patient_information: A 45-year-old male security guard from Malawi.
chief_complaint: Back pain and progressive difficulty in walking.
history_of_present_illness: Troubles started 1 year earlier with back pain which did not improve with paracetamol. Over weeks, he developed difficulty walking and 'pins and needles' in his legs, eventually becoming bedridden. He denies fever, night sweats, weight loss, chronic cough, haematuria, or diarrhoea.
exposure_and_epidemiology: Resides in an urban area, drinks about one litre of Chibuku per day, non-smoker, married with three children who are well. No history of trauma or past tuberculosis, never tested for HIV. Consulted a traditional healer who applied tattoos to his chest and back.
vitals: Afebrile with normal vital signs. Initial temperature was slightly elevated (37.5°C, 99.5°F) at first visit.
physical_exam: Tenderness over the lower thoracic spine with severe spasticity of both legs. Power in legs is 1/5 (visible muscle flicker). Deep tendon reflexes of lower limbs are exaggerated, plantar reflexes are upgoing. Sensory level for pain and temperature sensation between T9 and T11, with diminished joint sense in big toes bilaterally. Cranial nerves and upper limbs are normal.
labs_and_diagnostics: Full blood count results are normal. Urine dipstick normal, no ova of Schistosoma spp. in urine and stool. Spinal radiograph showed collapse of T11 vertebral body and soft tissue swelling around the spine. Chest radiography and abdominal ultrasound examination were normal. Found to be HIV-positive with a CD4 count of 331 cells/µL.
differential_diagnosis: Spinal TB ('Pott's disease'), spinal metastases, degenerative spinal disease (including slipped disc), schistosomiasis, autoimmune transverse myelitis, and HIV-associated vacuolar myelopathy.
management_and_clinical_course: Initially given paracetamol, antimalarials, a single dose of praziquantel, and paracetamol, without improvement. Later, a presumed diagnosis of spinal TB led to standard first-line antituberculous treatment, Vitamin B6, physiotherapy, and intensive guardian counselling. A spinal surgeon did not recommend immediate surgery but suggested a review in 3 months. The patient was discharged home with palliative care team involvement and started on antiretroviral therapy. At 3 months, he reported subjective improvement in gait, but neurological deficits remained unchanged and he was still waiting for a wheelchair.

tables.title: Important Causes of Spinal Cord Disease in the Tropics and Their Typical Clinical Features
rows: Insidious onset, chronically progressive over weeks, with months of back pain
Spasticity common, bladder may be spared, spinal deformity on examination
Subacute onset, chronically progressive over weeks
Spasticity or flaccidity, bladder may be spared
Acute (days) or subacute (a couple of weeks)
Often flaccid paresis, bladder involvement common
